correctness.rationale: The proof partitions every possible parent into an ordinary one-symbol insertion supersequence or a position-specific genuine split. The insertion sphere has exactly \(q+(n-1)(q-1)\) words by a canonical first-difference argument. A symbol has at most \(\binom{q-1}{2}\) genuine ordered splits, with equality at \(q-1\). This yields the upper bound, and the saturated received word makes the insertion and genuine-split families disjoint and attains it. The bundled verifier reconstructs the channel by two independent finite routes and checks the decomposition and formula. Source: RESULT.md and verify.py. Risk: finite checks alone are not an infinite proof, so acceptance relies on the analytic counting argument.
risks: Any flaw would have to occur in the insertion/genuine-split exhaustion or counting; both were separately reconstructed and finite-tested, but the universal quantifiers are discharged only by the written proof.

value.rationale: The quantity is the exact maximum incoming degree of the one-absorption channel incidence graph, equivalently the worst-case number of possible transmitted parents of a received word. That is a natural channel invariant relevant to ambiguity/list size and incidence-based coding bounds. The theorem holds for every alphabet size and block length and identifies an explicit extremal received word, so it is structural rather than an arbitrary finite slice. Sources: the primary paper motivates absorption-channel coding and uses incidence/hypergraph methods; RESULT.md gives the all-parameter theorem. Risk: the result does not by itself sharpen the best correcting-code redundancy bound and does not solve the separate forward-ball-size problem.
risks: No downstream optimal code theorem is claimed; value rests on the natural worst-case ambiguity/incoming-degree invariant itself.
